name: constructor-injection-not-globals
description: Tests explicit service dependencies and ownership rather than hidden mutable package state
prompt: I have a UserService that needs a database connection and a logger. What's the best way to set this up in Go? I was thinking of using a package-level var for the database.
trap: Hidden database lookup obscures ownership and makes test isolation difficult. A constructor fits this long-lived service; other APIs may use function parameters or configuration values.

assertions.text: Uses constructor injection (NewUserService taking dependencies as parameters)
Explicitly advises against package-level variables for service dependencies
Explains the ownership, hidden-dependency, or test-isolation costs of the proposed package-level database
Does NOT use init() for service initialization
Selects the constructor return type for the intended public contract

name: interface-defined-at-consumer
description: Tests that interfaces are defined where consumed, not where implemented
prompt: I'm building a Go service that uses a UserStore. Should I define the UserStore interface in the same package as the PostgreSQL implementation or somewhere else? Show me the correct pattern.
trap: Treats interface ownership as unconditional instead of considering package API requirements.

assertions.text: Shows a narrow consumer-owned interface as one suitable dependency seam
Explains that interface ownership depends on the intended contract
Allows a concrete return or an interface hiding a private implementation
Avoids requiring callers to depend on unneeded implementation details
Does not introduce an import cycle to declare interface satisfaction

name: container-not-passed-as-dependency
description: Tests resolved dependencies for business services rather than hidden container lookup
prompt: I'm using samber/do for DI in my Go project. My UserService needs a Database and a Mailer. Should I pass the do.Injector to UserService so it can look up what it needs?
trap: Passing an injector to this business service hides its Database and Mailer dependencies. Resolution belongs in wiring/provider code; explicit scope factories may also need container access.

assertions.text: Advises against passing the injector/container as a dependency
Identifies this as the service locator anti-pattern
Keeps injector use in wiring, providers, or explicit scope factories rather than ordinary UserService methods
Shows UserService receiving Database and Mailer directly as constructor parameters
Shows the provider function using do.MustInvoke inside the provider, not inside UserService methods

name: manual-di-for-small-projects
description: Tests whether straightforward service wiring justifies a DI library
prompt: I'm building a small Go REST API with about 5 services: config, database, user repository, user service, and HTTP handler. What DI approach should I use?
trap: A library adds registration and runtime failure modes. Evaluate the actual wiring and lifecycle needs without inventing a service-count threshold.

assertions.text: Recommends explicit manual wiring for the straightforward graph described
Does NOT recommend a DI library as the primary approach
Shows wiring in main() with explicit constructor calls in dependency order
Orders initialization according to actual dependencies rather than requiring named architectural layers
Chooses a library only for concrete lifecycle/wiring needs, not an arbitrary service-count threshold.

name: testing-with-di-mock-injection
description: Tests that DI enables testing by injecting mocks at the interface boundary
prompt: Write a test for a UserService that depends on a UserStore interface. The test should verify that GetUser returns the correct user when found and an error when not found. Don't use any DI library.
trap: Without the skill, the model may test with a real database or skip the mock pattern. The skill requires mocking at the interface boundary.

assertions.text: Creates a mock implementation of the UserStore interface
Injects the mock into UserService via the constructor (NewUserService)
Tests both the success path (user found) and the error path (not found)
Does NOT use a real database connection in the test
The mock is defined in the test file, not as a package-level or global variable

name: shallow-dependency-graph
description: Tests that deep dependency chains are flagged as a design problem
prompt: My Go application has this dependency chain: Config -> Database -> UserRepo -> UserService -> NotificationService -> OrderService -> PaymentService -> APIHandler. Is this a good architecture?
trap: Without the skill, the model may accept this deep chain as normal layered architecture. The skill says deep chains signal design problems and recommends flattening.

assertions.text: Identifies the deep dependency chain as a design problem
Recommends flattening the dependency graph
Suggests that most services should depend on repositories and config directly, not transitively through other services
Explains the negative consequences of deep chains (fragility, hard to test, or hard to maintain)
Proposes a concrete restructuring where OrderService and PaymentService don't depend on each other transitively

name: one-container-per-app-not-per-request
description: Tests that a DI container is created once per application, not per request
prompt: I'm building a Go HTTP API with samber/do. In each HTTP handler, I'm creating a new do.New() injector, providing all services, then invoking the one I need. This way each request gets fresh services. Is this correct?
trap: Recreating the whole application graph per request can discard pooling and lifecycle ownership. Share application resources and scope request state deliberately; request-scoped containers are not inherently invalid.

assertions.text: Identifies creating a new container per request as a mistake
Recommends one container per application created at startup
Explains the performance or correctness problem with per-request containers (recreating singletons, no connection reuse)
Suggests using scopes for request-level isolation if needed
Shows the container being created once in main() and services injected into handlers

name: lazy-vs-eager-initialization
description: Chooses initialization and lifetime from behavior.
prompt: When using a DI container in Go, should all my services be created at application startup? I have a database pool, a cache client, and some request processing services.
trap: Assumes lazy always wins or stateless services must be transient.

assertions.text: Weighs early startup validation against deferring optional expensive work.
Shares concurrency-safe database pools and cache clients with an explicit shutdown owner.
Allows shared stateless services; transient is not inherently required by statelessness.
Explains lazy initialization moves failures and latency to first use.
Uses the actual installed container API rather than treating all DI libraries as equivalent.
